title: September story bank
purpose: Expository and original oratory topic selection, reviewed for evidence, logic, impact and age suitability.

definitions.impact: Scale, severity and duration of effects on people or institutions. Credible potential effects are distinguished from observed effects.
definitions.weirdness: A surprising mechanism, contradiction or reversal, not the entertainment value of suffering.
definitions.accessibility: Background knowledge and emotional readiness needed for students aged 8–16. Read alongside minimum-age guidance.
definitions.expository: Potential to explain a meaningful mechanism clearly, accurately and memorably, with a useful structure or visual.
definitions.oratory: Potential for an original, defensible thesis with relatable stakes, narrative, counterargument and a proportionate call to action.
definitions.logic: Strength of the evidence-to-claim-to-impact chain; scope for honest causal reasoning and handling objections. Not agreement with a political viewpoint.

notes: Scores are editorial judgments for student-topic coaching, not official tournament rubrics or predictions of winning.
All 100 stories are ranked across five lenses: overall, expository, original oratory, logic and impact, and unusualness.
Minimum age is coaching guidance based on context and sensitivity. Ages 8–11 should use the younger adaptation only where recommended.
New studies and substantive investigations published in September qualify. Older underlying events are identified, and proposals, predictions and claims are not presented as completed outcomes.
A speech needs more than a headline. Original oratory should develop the student’s own thesis; expository should explain rather than quietly turn into advocacy.
Impact claims need a mechanism, affected group, scale and timeframe. Avoid claiming one story proves a universal trend.
Source access and evidence status refer to this research snapshot. Links and breaking-news facts may change later.
Ties use impact, then logic, then title. Small numerical differences should not override a student’s interest or experience.
The ranking is a transparent editorial judgment using the displayed weights. It supports topic selection and does not measure news importance objectively.
